turns.reply:
This campaign targets customers who are eligible for OS-to-EMI but have never started a request, and tries to move more of them to a Successful EMI Request. Because the platform has no event or attribute that marks 'OS-to-EMI eligible, never started,' the audience can only be approximated through an issuer-configured Smart Tag whose existence I cannot verify from here. The core mechanism is a controlled test of two cost-framings (affordability vs. total-cost transparency) addressing the user's interest-cost hesitation belief, rather than guessing which framing is right.

**Approaches considered**
- **Account-level audience segment, framing experiment** — chosen
  Entry: Audience entry on Account: Status = Active, Smart Tag = <issuer-configured 'OS-to-EMI eligible, never started' tag — existence unverified>
  Mechanism: Two-arm experiment testing cost-framing (affordability vs. total-cost transparency), with a channel-fallback branch if the opening email is not delivered
  Timing: Fixed-interval drip (48h minimum spacing) from entry, EMAIL first then SMS/WHATSAPP, since no per-customer event anchors a 'near due date' trigger
  Trade-off: Matches the user's actual audience definition (a standing eligibility state, not a one-off event) but depends on an unverified Smart Tag existing; cannot personalise timing to each customer's real statement due date
  Why this one: The user defined the audience as a standing state ('eligible but never started'), not an event. Only an audience-segment entry can express a standing state; an event-triggered entry would necessarily fire on something that happened, which is the wrong shape for 'never happened yet.'
- Transaction-eligibility event trigger
  Entry: Event entry on Transaction Events: Transaction, EMI Eligible = true, Transaction Status in SETTLED/APPROVED
  Mechanism: Same cost-framing experiment, triggered the moment an EMI-eligible purchase is made
  Timing: Event-triggered, fires near the moment of opportunity on a specific purchase
  Trade-off: Reliably buildable and confirmed-reachable as an event, but it targets people with one EMI-eligible transaction — closer to Txn-to-EMI eligibility — not customers with a qualifying revolving outstanding balance. Using it would silently reach a different population than 'OS-to-EMI eligible,' at a different grain (one purchase vs. a running balance).

**Approach**
- Audience = never-started eligible customers: decided by user, stated directly.
- Goal = EMI_STATUS_CHANGED with Source=OS-to-EMI and New Status=Successful: rests on tool-confirmed allowed values; this is the only event that proves the behaviour the user described ('EMI Requests reaching Successful').
- Entry via Account Smart Tag rather than a Transaction eligibility event: my judgement, because the alternative (Transaction EMI Eligible=true) measures a different, narrower thing than the audience the user defined — flagged as a limitation, not resolved by substitution.
- Cost-framing experiment rather than asking the user to pick a single interest-cost narrative: my judgement, because the user cannot reliably know which sub-driver (rate, total cost, tenure, limit impact) dominates, and a controlled test can establish it where a guess cannot.
- Channel order EMAIL→SMS→WHATSAPP: rests on tenant preference (prefer lower-cost channel first, P-010), reserving WhatsApp for recovery/reinforcement.
- 48-hour spacing and 4-message cap: hard constraints from the tenant's operational configuration, not negotiable.

**Options weighed**
- Segmentation — used. The journey splits customers into two framing arms; a further balance-based segment (the >₹25,000 hunch) is a named but currently unbuildable segmentation, carried as an open item rather than dropped.
- Experimentation — used. Two real arms with real copy test affordability-framing vs. total-cost-transparency framing — the two most plausible readings of 'interest-cost hesitation' — read by comparing Successful-conversion counts per arm, changing exactly one variable (P-005).
- Conditional branching — used. After the opening email, a condition on its delivery outcome branches customers down a different path depending on whether the email was actually delivered/engaged.
- Channel fallback — used. The condition's 'No' branch (email not delivered) escalates to SMS then WhatsApp; the 'Yes' branch (delivered) continues on the cheaper SMS reminder. Built as an explicit condition+branch, since a per-send fallback property is not available on this platform.
- Adaptive sequencing — not applicable here. No reliable per-customer signal exists to age the message or channel against (no due-date event, no eligibility-recency signal); the branching above is a one-time delivery-outcome split, not sequencing that adapts over time.
- Cost and fatigue — used. Capped at 2 sends on the engaged path and 3 on the recovery path, both under the 4-message cap. The weakest message is the final WhatsApp nudge on the recovery path — kept because it is the only touch left for customers whose email never delivered, but it is the first one I would cut if fatigue becomes a concern.
- Measurement and learning — used. The experiment arms are randomised against each other, so a difference in Successful-conversion rate between them can be reasonably attributed to the framing (P-005/P-006). A 10% control group (tenant's stated preference) is included so the campaign's effect versus no messaging at all can also be read, not just arm-vs-arm.

**Considered and not used**
- Transaction-eligibility event entry (Architecture 2) — Buildable and reachable, but it identifies a single EMI-eligible purchase, not a customer carrying a qualifying outstanding balance — a different population at a different grain than the audience the user asked for.

**Success criteria**
- More EMI Requests reaching 'Successful' status (Source = OS-to-EMI) among the never-started-eligible audience — this is the business's own measure, stated as no fixed numeric target.

**Measurement**
- Track EMI_STATUS_CHANGED → Successful (Source=OS-to-EMI) counts per experiment arm and against the 10% control group.
- Track email delivery/open outcomes to see how many customers fall into the fallback (non-delivered) branch versus the engaged branch.
- Read arm-vs-arm difference as evidence about framing, not as a campaign-wide lift claim, unless compared against the control group.
- To measure the >₹25,000 balance hunch properly, the bank would need a running-balance attribute on Account or EMI Request (or a verified Smart Tag) — currently absent.

**Assumptions**
- DNC suppression and NPA exclusion are enforced by the platform at send time regardless of blueprint conditions, per tenant configuration.
- The Account Smart Tag used for entry is assumed to exist and to mean 'OS-to-EMI eligible, never started a request' — unverified from here.
- Statement Due Date cannot be used as a dynamic per-customer trigger in this entry shape, so 'urgency near due date' is approximated with fixed 48h spacing rather than true due-date personalisation.

**Hypotheses for future testing**
- Affordability framing (smaller monthly payment) converts differently than total-cost-transparency framing for interest-cost-hesitant customers — untested.
- Customers with outstanding balances above ₹25,000 convert at a different rate than those below — untested and currently unmeasurable on this platform.

**Worth settling before this is built**
- The >₹25,000 outstanding-balance hunch cannot be targeted today (no balance attribute exists). Do you want to pursue an issuer-configured Smart Tag that encodes this threshold (if one could be built), or proceed without balance segmentation and treat it as a hypothesis to examine later from reporting? This decides whether the campaign can act on the user's own hunch about which customers convert better, or whether it reaches a broader, unsegmented eligible population and the hunch stays unproven. Until then: Proceed without balance segmentation; the hunch is recorded as an untested hypothesis, not targeted.

**Defaults applied**
- Channel order and escalation path for the fallback branch. Affects cost only, not who is reached. Until then: Default: EMAIL first (lowest cost), SMS for engaged-path reminder, SMS then WhatsApp escalation for the non-delivered path, per tenant preference to lead with lower-cost channels.

**Limitations**
- EMI Events is marked new in the platform metadata: proposed, not confirmed as built in production. This campaign depends on it, so it cannot be presented as a verified platform capability.
- EMI_STATUS_CHANGED (the goal event) and Transaction (the rejected-architecture's event) are both marked 'new-proposed' in platform metadata — not confirmed as built in production. If EMI_STATUS_CHANGED is not actually live, the goal cannot be tracked and the campaign cannot report Successful conversions at all.
- If a customer starts (but does not complete) an OS-to-EMI request mid-campaign, the builder has no way to detect that mid-journey (condition steps only read a previous send's delivery outcome, not EMI Request status) and divert them to a different message. Such customers will keep receiving 'never started' messaging until/unless they reach Successful (which auto-exits them via the platform's goal check). They won't be mistargeted with false claims, but the messaging may feel slightly stale to them.

**Cannot be generated yet**
- steps[0].experiment.arms[0][1].condition: 2 open slots exist; the continuation is ambiguous.
- steps[0].experiment.arms[1][1].condition: 2 open slots exist; the continuation is ambiguous.

**Cannot be verified by the platform**
- Smart Tag is an issuer-configured Smart Tag. The platform metadata holds no list of real tag values, so "OS_TO_EMI_ELIGIBLE_NOT_STARTED" cannot be verified here.

**Still unknown**
- Whether an issuer-configured Smart Tag exists at all for this eligibility definition, and whether it can also encode the >₹25,000 balance hunch.
- Whether EMI_STATUS_CHANGED and Transaction events are actually live in production (both marked 'new-proposed' in platform metadata) — the goal depends on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED being live.

architectures.name: Transaction-eligibility event trigger
architectures.entry: Event entry on Transaction Events: Transaction, EMI Eligible = true, Transaction Status in SETTLED/APPROVED
architectures.mechanism: Same cost-framing experiment, triggered the moment an EMI-eligible purchase is made
architectures.timing: Event-triggered, fires near the moment of opportunity on a specific purchase
architectures.tradeoff: Reliably buildable and confirmed-reachable as an event, but it targets people with one EMI-eligible transaction — closer to Txn-to-EMI eligibility — not customers with a qualifying revolving outstanding balance. Using it would silently reach a different population than 'OS-to-EMI eligible,' at a different grain (one purchase vs. a running balance).

approach: Audience = never-started eligible customers: decided by user, stated directly.

Goal = EMI_STATUS_CHANGED with Source=OS-to-EMI and New Status=Successful: rests on tool-confirmed allowed values; this is the only event that proves the behaviour the user described ('EMI Requests reaching Successful').

Entry via Account Smart Tag rather than a Transaction eligibility event: my judgement, because the alternative (Transaction EMI Eligible=true) measures a different, narrower thing than the audience the user defined — flagged as a limitation, not resolved by substitution.

Cost-framing experiment rather than asking the user to pick a single interest-cost narrative: my judgement, because the user cannot reliably know which sub-driver (rate, total cost, tenure, limit impact) dominates, and a controlled test can establish it where a guess cannot.
Channel order EMAIL→SMS→WHATSAPP: rests on tenant preference (prefer lower-cost channel first, P-010), reserving WhatsApp for recovery/reinforcement.
48-hour spacing and 4-message cap: hard constraints from the tenant's operational configuration, not negotiable.

strategyOptions.why: The journey splits customers into two framing arms; a further balance-based segment (the >₹25,000 hunch) is a named but currently unbuildable segmentation, carried as an open item rather than dropped.

Two real arms with real copy test affordability-framing vs. total-cost-transparency framing — the two most plausible readings of 'interest-cost hesitation' — read by comparing Successful-conversion counts per arm, changing exactly one variable (P-005).
After the opening email, a condition on its delivery outcome branches customers down a different path depending on whether the email was actually delivered/engaged.

The condition's 'No' branch (email not delivered) escalates to SMS then WhatsApp; the 'Yes' branch (delivered) continues on the cheaper SMS reminder. Built as an explicit condition+branch, since a per-send fallback property is not available on this platform.

No reliable per-customer signal exists to age the message or channel against (no due-date event, no eligibility-recency signal); the branching above is a one-time delivery-outcome split, not sequencing that adapts over time.

Capped at 2 sends on the engaged path and 3 on the recovery path, both under the 4-message cap. The weakest message is the final WhatsApp nudge on the recovery path — kept because it is the only touch left for customers whose email never delivered, but it is the first one I would cut if fatigue becomes a concern.

The experiment arms are randomised against each other, so a difference in Successful-conversion rate between them can be reasonably attributed to the framing (P-005/P-006). A 10% control group (tenant's stated preference) is included so the campaign's effect versus no messaging at all can also be read, not just arm-vs-arm.

rejected.why: Buildable and reachable, but it identifies a single EMI-eligible purchase, not a customer carrying a qualifying outstanding balance — a different population at a different grain than the audience the user asked for.

successCriteria: More EMI Requests reaching 'Successful' status (Source = OS-to-EMI) among the never-started-eligible audience — this is the business's own measure, stated as no fixed numeric target.
measurement: Track EMI_STATUS_CHANGED → Successful (Source=OS-to-EMI) counts per experiment arm and against the 10% control group.
Track email delivery/open outcomes to see how many customers fall into the fallback (non-delivered) branch versus the engaged branch.
Read arm-vs-arm difference as evidence about framing, not as a campaign-wide lift claim, unless compared against the control group.
To measure the >₹25,000 balance hunch properly, the bank would need a running-balance attribute on Account or EMI Request (or a verified Smart Tag) — currently absent.
assumptions: DNC suppression and NPA exclusion are enforced by the platform at send time regardless of blueprint conditions, per tenant configuration.
The Account Smart Tag used for entry is assumed to exist and to mean 'OS-to-EMI eligible, never started a request' — unverified from here.
Statement Due Date cannot be used as a dynamic per-customer trigger in this entry shape, so 'urgency near due date' is approximated with fixed 48h spacing rather than true due-date personalisation.
unknowns: Whether an issuer-configured Smart Tag exists at all for this eligibility definition, and whether it can also encode the >₹25,000 balance hunch.
Whether EMI_STATUS_CHANGED and Transaction events are actually live in production (both marked 'new-proposed' in platform metadata) — the goal depends on EMI_STATUS_CHANGED being live.
hypotheses: Affordability framing (smaller monthly payment) converts differently than total-cost-transparency framing for interest-cost-hesitant customers — untested.
Customers with outstanding balances above ₹25,000 convert at a different rate than those below — untested and currently unmeasurable on this platform.

dimensions.rationale: The platform can only target the first group precisely (EMI_STATUS_CHANGED / New Status=Pending / Source=OS-to-EMI). The second group has no eligibility event or verified attribute. This changes the entry event, the audience, and whether the campaign is a completion-nudge or an awareness/offer campaign.
dimensions.note: Resolved: campaign targets customers who are eligible but have never started an OS-to-EMI request. The in-flight/pending-request track is explicitly out of scope for this campaign.

dimensions.name: Perceived barrier to conversion
dimensions.rationale: Whether customers don't know the option exists, worry about cost/tenure, or abandon mid-process determines whether the message should educate, reassure on cost, or simply remind-and-link back to the in-progress request.
dimensions.note: User's own explanation ('interest-cost hesitation'), not a finding. It bundles several distinct drivers (rate, total payable, tenure, limit impact) that imply different copy. The user is unlikely to know which sub-driver dominates, so this is resolved by TESTING two competing cost-framings against each other rather than asking the user to guess — see Experimentation in strategyOptions. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.

dimensions.name: Outstanding balance / ticket size
dimensions.rationale: Larger outstanding balances may warrant a different urgency or framing than small ones, and may deserve separate treatment. Holding this open until the audience-stage fork is resolved, since it only matters once we know which population we're addressing.
dimensions.note: Confirmed via list_audience_attributes: neither Account nor EMI Request carries a balance/amount field. Transaction Amount is a single purchase's value, not the customer's running outstanding balance — using it would target a different thing at a different grain, so it is not used as a substitute. The >₹25,000 hunch cannot be targeted on this platform today; it is carried as an untested hypothesis and raised as an open item below rather than quietly dropped or approximated.

dimensions.name: Request urgency window
dimensions.rationale: An EMI Request (Pending) expires after 7 days (P-003, verified). This is a hard timing constraint on any in-flight-recovery design, not something to ask about.
dimensions.note: P-003: once a request is opened it stays live up to 7 days before Expired. Less directly binding on this never-started audience (no request exists yet), but it bounds how long any post-start recovery would have, and bounds our own send sequence comfortably (total journey length here is under 4 days).

turns.reply: Two things changed this round. First, your repeated statement ('what we actually care about is customers not going dormant') does answer how you want success judged: not raw login volume, but fewer customers slipping into dormancy — I've recorded that. Second, I checked the platform's actual data and found something material: Account.Status has a real, usable value of 'Dormant' (alongside Active, Closed, Suspended, etc.) — so 'dormant' is not a vague idea here, it's a concrete, buildable account state. That turns the audience question from abstract into a genuine fork with two very different, both-buildable campaigns: (A) catch accounts BEFORE they go Dormant — entry on Account.Status = Active, broad reach, prevention framing; or (B) win back accounts that are ALREADY Dormant — entry on Account.Status = Dormant, narrower reach, reactivation framing. These have different audiences, different entry condition, and different message ('keep doing what you're doing' vs 'come back, here's what you're missing'), so I can't default one on your behalf. turns.reply: Abandoned card application recovery is a well-understood pattern, but three things are genuinely unsettled and each would point to a different campaign. First, nobody has told me how the bank itself will judge this working — that measure is the business's to give, not mine to assume, and it has to be set before I design the goal or the message cadence. Second, the platform's funnel-stage events (Journey Progress / Pageload / Button Click with a locked Status/Page/Button attribute) could represent very different points in the application — KYC, document upload, offer selection, final review — and if drop-off concentrates at one stage rather than spreading evenly, the entry condition, the message content, and even the channel choice should target that stage specifically rather than 'anyone mid-application'. Third, the mechanism I'd recommend (remove friction vs. remind vs. resurface a benefit) depends entirely on why the bank believes people stop; a KYC delay, a document-upload hassle, and cold feet about the card terms are three different problems needing three different messages, and only the bank has seen enough real applicants to have a working theory. I checked the event catalogue, the audience attribute catalogue, the channel list, the step-type catalogue and template availability before asking — none of them can answer these three, they're business-side.
